trad_Dispensational: Christ's return is soon from heaven's perspective; the promise is imminent.
trad_Academic: The closing prayer of the Revelation; 'Maranatha' is among the earliest Aramaic liturgical expressions in Christianity.

text: When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
desc: Hosea's prophecy of Israel called out of Egypt, cited by Matthew as fulfilled in the Holy Family's return from Egypt.
hebrewKey: בְּנִי (beni) — my son; used of both national Israel and, by Matthew's pesher, of Christ
archaeology: The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC, Cairo Museum) provides the earliest extrabiblical mention of Israel.
trad_Jewish: Classic corporate reference to the Exodus. The nation Israel is God's firstborn son (Exod 4:22). No Messianic reading in mainstream rabbinic sources.
trad_Catholic: Matthew 2:15 is a typological fulfillment — Christ recapitulates Israel's history. The Magisterium upholds both senses (literal historical + typological).
trad_Protestant: Matthew's use is typological/pesher exegesis. Christ as the true Israel relives the Exodus pattern. Common in Reformed covenant theology.
trad_Dispensational: Israel and Christ both called 'son'; Matthew applies a sensus plenior. The double fulfillment is characteristic of prophetic telescoping.
trad_Academic: Classic example of NT pesher — Matthew recontextualizes a corporate historical statement about Israel as a Messianic proof text. Not predictive in its original context (Gundry, Matthew, 1982).

text: After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his sight.
desc: Hosea's third-day resurrection language applied by Paul and early Christians to Christ's resurrection on the third day.
hebrewKey: בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי (yom ha-shelishi) — on the third day; a key phrase in Paul's kerygma
trad_Jewish: Read as national restoration after Assyrian judgment — revival of Israel as a people. Not Messianic in standard rabbinic interpretation.
trad_Catholic: Patristic tradition (Origen, Jerome) sees this as prophetic of the resurrection on the third day, fulfilling Paul's 'according to the Scriptures' (1 Cor 15:4).
trad_Protestant: Paul's 'according to the Scriptures' likely alludes here. Corporate Israel's restoration is a type of Christ's resurrection.
trad_Academic: Paul's kerygma formula (1 Cor 15:3-4) cites 'Scriptures' for the third day. Scholars debate whether Hosea 6:2 is the referent (Allison, 1985) or whether no specific text is intended.

keywords: David's tent|restore|rebuild|David's fallen booth/shelter|ruins|Gentiles called|possess nations
text: In that day will I raise up the tabernacle of David that is fallen, and close up the breaches thereof; and I will raise up his ruins, and I will build it as in the days of old:
desc: The restoration of David's fallen tent, cited by James at Jerusalem Council as fulfilled in Gentile inclusion through Christ.
hebrewKey: סֻכַּת דָּוִיד (sukkat David) — booth/tent of David; symbolic of the Davidic dynasty
archaeology: The Tel Dan Inscription (9th c. BC, Israel Museum) confirms the Davidic dynasty's historicity as 'House of David'.
trad_Jewish: Future restoration of the Davidic kingdom and Temple worship. Major eschatological hope — particularly prominent in Rosh Hashanah liturgy.
trad_Catholic: James cites this at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15) as fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and the inclusion of Gentiles in the Church.
trad_Protestant: Fulfilled at Pentecost and the formation of the Church. The 'fallen tent' is the Davidic line restored in Christ.
trad_Dispensational: Partially fulfilled in the Church Age; fully fulfilled in the literal Millennial Kingdom under David's throne.
trad_Academic: James's use at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) is the earliest surviving Christian interpretation. The Hebrew sukkat is variously translated; LXX reads 'tabernacle'.

text: And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the Lord GOD, that I will cause the sun to go down at noon, and I will darken the earth in the clear day:
desc: The darkening of the sun at noon, fulfilled at the crucifixion when darkness covered the land from noon to 3pm.
hebrewKey: הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בַּצָּהֳרַיִם (ha-shemesh ba-tsohorayim) — the sun at noon
trad_Jewish: Historical judgment oracle against Israel. The darkness is metaphorical — social and political upheaval, not a literal astronomical event.
trad_Catholic: The three-hour darkness at the crucifixion (noon–3pm) fulfills this sign of divine judgment. Cited by Church Fathers including Origen.
trad_Protestant: The crucifixion darkness is a fulfillment of cosmic signs associated with judgment. Christ bears the judgment meant for Israel.
trad_Academic: Original context: judgment against Israel's northern kingdom. Crucifixion darkness may have been a natural phenomenon (eclipse, sandstorm) given theological interpretation by evangelists.

keywords: shepherd|flock|strength|LORD|ends of the earth|majesty|name of the LORD|secure|Bethlehem king|greatness
text: And he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God; and they shall abide: for now shall he be great unto the ends of the earth. feed or, rule
desc: The ruler from Bethlehem shepherding in the LORD's strength and being great to the ends of the earth.
hebrewKey: רָעָה (ra'ah) — to shepherd/graze; combined with עַד־אַפְסֵי אָרֶץ — to the ends of the earth
trad_Jewish: The Messianic ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2) exercises worldwide dominion as shepherd-king. Key eschatological text in rabbinic Messianism.
trad_Catholic: Fulfilled in Christ as the Good Shepherd whose Petrine Church shepherds the flock to the ends of the earth.
trad_Protestant: Christ's worldwide rule through the Church and ultimately in the New Creation.
trad_Dispensational: Initial fulfillment in Christ's ministry; full fulfillment in the Millennial reign from Jerusalem.
trad_Academic: Continuation of the Micah 5:2 oracle. The 'shepherd' is a common ANE royal metaphor (cf. Hammurabi). Global dominion is hyperbolic for the oracle's immediate context.

text: But with an overrunning flood he will make an utter end of the place thereof, and darkness shall pursue his enemies.
desc: Nineveh's complete and final destruction, fulfilled when the Medes and Babylonians destroyed it in 612 BC.
hebrewKey: שֶׁטֶף עֹבֵר (shetef over) — overwhelming/passing flood; literal flooding preceded Nineveh's fall
archaeology: Nineveh fell to Babylon and Media in 612 BC. Kuyunjik mound excavations (Layard, 1849; ongoing) reveal destruction layers. Ancient sources (Diodorus Siculus) confirm the Tigris flooded the city walls before its fall.
trad_Jewish: Fulfilled historically — Nineveh was destroyed in 612 BC exactly as predicted. Celebrated as divine justice for Assyrian brutality against Israel.
trad_Catholic: A model of fulfilled predictive prophecy. The precision of Nahum's details (flood, complete destruction) validates divine foreknowledge.
trad_Protestant: One of the most literally fulfilled prophecies in Scripture. Nineveh's destruction vindicates Nahum's authenticity against late-dating critics.
trad_Academic: Ancient sources confirm a flood preceded the fall. However, critical scholars date Nahum to near the events — possibly post-eventu. The Nineveh destruction layer is archaeologically confirmed.

text: For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.
desc: The ultimate global knowledge of God's glory, partially inaugurated in the gospel age, fully realized in the new creation.
hebrewKey: תִּמָּלֵא הָאָרֶץ לָדַעַת (timale ha-aretz la-daat) — the earth will be filled to know; echoes Isaiah 11:9
trad_Jewish: Eschatological hope — the Messianic age when Torah knowledge fills the world. Central to Jewish universalist eschatology.
trad_Catholic: Progressively fulfilled through the Church's evangelization; fully at the Parousia.
trad_Protestant: Being fulfilled through global gospel proclamation; fully at the consummation.
trad_Academic: Draws on Isaiah 11:9 tradition. Part of the 'golden age' prophetic genre common in ANE literature.

text: I will declare the decree: the LORD hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee.
desc: The decree of divine Sonship cited in Hebrews 1:5 and Acts 13:33 as fulfilled in Christ's resurrection and exaltation.
hebrewKey: בְּנִי אַתָּה (beni attah) — You are my son; אֲנִי הַיּוֹם יְלִדְתִּיךָ (ani ha-yom yelidticha) — today I have begotten you
archaeology: Psalm 2 uses ANE royal coronation language attested in Egyptian and Mesopotamian enthronement texts.
trad_Jewish: A royal Psalm for David's coronation. Targumic tradition sees 'my son' as referring to the Messiah-King. The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) discusses messianic interpretations.
trad_Catholic: Fulfilled in Christ's baptism, transfiguration, and resurrection. 'Today' in Hebrews 1:5 refers to the eternal generation of the Son.
trad_Protestant: Fulfilled at the resurrection — Paul explicitly cites this in Acts 13:33 as fulfilled at Christ's resurrection. Also applicable to the baptism.
trad_Oneness: 'This day have I begotten thee' is not eternal generation, and it does not point first to Bethlehem: Paul preaches it of the resurrection (Acts 13:33) and Hebrews of the glorified High Priest (Heb. 5:5). The one God was manifest in flesh as a true man — Son from birth — and at the appointed day the Father declared that born Son the ruling Son, with all authority in His household. The begetting here is enthronement, not the origin of a second person.
trad_Academic: Originally a Davidic coronation Psalm. The NT applies it christologically via pesher/typology. Hebrews 1:5 is the most developed theological use.

text: Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him.
desc: Psalm 72's vision of universal royal submission to the Messianic king, fulfilled in Christ's universal lordship.
hebrewKey: כָּל־מְלָכִים יִשְׁתַּחֲווּ (kol-melakhim yishtachavu) — all kings will bow down
trad_Jewish: The ideal Solomonic kingdom extended to include all nations. Eschatologically the Messiah-King receives universal homage.
trad_Catholic: Being fulfilled in Christ's reign through the Church; completely at the Parousia. The liturgy anticipates this cosmic lordship.
trad_Protestant: Already/not-yet: Christ is Lord now; all creation will acknowledge it at the Second Coming (Phil 2:10-11).
trad_Dispensational: Fulfilled literally in the Millennial Kingdom when all surviving nations submit to Christ reigning from Jerusalem.
trad_Academic: Royal Psalm for Solomon using standard ANE hyperbole for universal dominion (cf. Psalm 89, Egyptian royal texts). Universal scope is court ideology, not prediction.

text: I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah.
desc: The Davidic covenant's eternal throne promise, fulfilled in Christ's eternal kingdom on David's throne.
hebrewKey: כָּרַתִּי בְרִית (karati berit) — I have cut a covenant; עַד־עוֹלָם (ad-olam) — forever
archaeology: The Tel Dan Inscription (9th c. BC) and the Mesha Stele both confirm the historical Davidic dynasty.
trad_Jewish: The Davidic covenant is the cornerstone of Messianic expectation. The Talmud debates whether the covenant is conditional or unconditional given the exile.
trad_Catholic: Fulfilled in Christ, Son of David. The incarnation and resurrection establish the eternal Davidic throne.
trad_Protestant: Christ is the promised Davidic heir whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32-33). The Davidic covenant finds its telos in Christ.
trad_Academic: Psalm 89 struggles with the apparent failure of the Davidic covenant post-exile. The lament section (vv. 38-52) questions the covenant's validity — an honest theological tension.

text: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
desc: The rejected capstone becoming the cornerstone, cited by Jesus, Peter, and Paul as fulfilled in Christ's rejection and exaltation.
hebrewKey: אֶבֶן מָאֲסוּ הַבּוֹנִים (even ma'asu ha-bonim) — the stone the builders rejected; רֹאשׁ פִּנָּה (rosh pinnah) — head of the corner
trad_Jewish: Originally applied to Israel — rejected among the nations, yet chosen by God. Sung at Passover (Hallel, Ps 113-118). The Talmud (Pesachim 119a) preserves discussion.
trad_Catholic: Jesus explicitly identifies himself as this stone (Matt 21:42). Peter's citation before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:11) is bold. The cornerstone of the Church.
trad_Protestant: One of the most clearly self-applied Messianic texts — Jesus cites it of himself. The rejected Messiah becomes the foundation.
trad_Oneness: The rejected stone is Jesus, who is YHWH — "this is the LORD's doing" (v.23). The cornerstone is not a second divine person placed by the Father but YHWH himself rejected by his own people and vindicated in resurrection.
trad_Academic: Originally a national/community Psalm. Jesus' self-application in the Temple (Mark 12:10) is historically attested by multiple sources. Peter's use in Acts is early Christian apologetic.

text: Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him; and I will loose the loins of kings, to open before him the two leaved gates; and the gates shall not be shut;
desc: Cyrus named by name 150 years before his birth as the one who would release Israel from Babylon.
hebrewKey: מָשִׁיחוֹ (meshicho) — his anointed one; applied uniquely to the pagan king Cyrus; כּוֹרֶשׁ (Koresh) — Cyrus
archaeology: The Cyrus Cylinder (539 BC, British Museum BM 90920) records Cyrus's decree allowing conquered peoples to return to their homelands. Josephus (Ant. 11.1) records Cyrus read Isaiah's prophecy.
trad_Jewish: A remarkable prophecy naming a Gentile ruler 150+ years before his birth. Jewish tradition holds Isaiah wrote this in the 8th century — a divine foreknowledge claim.
trad_Catholic: Classic predictive prophecy. Josephus records that Cyrus was shown this text and fulfilled it consciously. Cyrus as 'anointed' is typologically related to Messianic anointing.
trad_Protestant: The naming of Cyrus is a primary argument for the unity of Isaiah (chs. 1-66) vs. Deutero-Isaiah hypothesis.
trad_Academic: A key text in the Isaiah authorship debate. Critical scholars date chs. 40-55 to c. 550-540 BC (Deutero-Isaiah), making the Cyrus reference contemporary — not predictive. The Cylinder confirms the historical liberation.

text: Who hath heard such a thing? who hath seen such things? Shall the earth be made to bring forth in one day? or shall a nation be born at once? for as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children.
desc: A nation born in a day, widely applied to Israel's rebirth on May 14, 1948, in fulfillment of prophetic expectation.
hebrewKey: אֶרֶץ בְּיוֹם אֶחָד (eretz be-yom echad) — a land in one day; גּוֹי פַּעַם אֶחָת (goi pa'am achat) — a nation at once
archaeology: Israel declared independence May 14, 1948 — recognized within 11 minutes by the US. The UN partition plan, British Mandate records, and news archives document the single-day proclamation.
trad_Jewish: The restoration of Israel in 1948 is widely seen in modern Jewish thought as fulfillment, though the text is originally about Zion's miraculous restoration after exile.
trad_Catholic: Points to the eschatological gathering of Israel — both the 1948 event and the final ingathering at the Parousia are typologically related.
trad_Protestant: Israel's 1948 rebirth is a modern fulfillment of this text and of Ezekiel's dry bones vision.
trad_Dispensational: One of the most remarkable modern fulfillments — a nation reborn in a single day after 1,878 years of statelessness, exactly as predicted.
trad_Academic: The original context is the restoration of Zion post-exile. Application to 1948 is modern theological interpretation. The rhetorical question underscores the miraculous nature of divine restoration.

text: For thus saith the LORD, That after seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
desc: Jeremiah's 70-year Babylonian captivity promise, fulfilled exactly when Cyrus issued the edict in 538 BC.
hebrewKey: שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה (shivim shanah) — seventy years; the same phrase appears in Daniel 9:2 as Daniel reads this text
archaeology: The Babylonian Chronicles (British Museum) document the fall of Jerusalem (597 BC, 586 BC) and Cyrus's conquest of Babylon (539 BC). The 70-year period is historically confirmed.
trad_Jewish: A precisely fulfilled prophecy. Daniel reads Jeremiah and calculates the end of the exile (Dan 9:2). The Talmud (Megillah 11b) discusses the counting.
trad_Catholic: A model of literal predictive fulfillment — the 70 years from the first deportation (605 BC) to Cyrus's edict (536 BC) is approximately fulfilled.
trad_Protestant: A clear literal fulfillment confirming Jeremiah's divine inspiration. Daniel's study of it demonstrates the early recognition of Jeremiah as prophetic Scripture.
trad_Academic: The 70-year figure likely draws on Mesopotamian traditions of desolation periods. The historical fulfillment is broadly confirmed, though debate continues about precise starting/ending dates.

text: And say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land:
desc: The regathering of Israel from all nations to their own land, partially fulfilled in 1948 and ongoing.
hebrewKey: וְקִבַּצְתִּי אֹתָם (ve-kibatzti otam) — I will gather them; גּוֹי אֶחָד (goy echad) — one nation
archaeology: Modern aliyah (Jewish immigration) statistics (Jewish Agency), the UN partition vote, and 1948 Declaration of Independence all document the literal gathering from 100+ nations.
trad_Jewish: The modern State of Israel is seen as partial fulfillment. The full regathering awaits the Messianic era.
trad_Catholic: Points to both the post-exilic return and the eschatological ingathering of Israel.
trad_Protestant: Being fulfilled — the 1948 return and continuing aliyah are stages in God's prophetic program.
trad_Dispensational: The modern regathering is the greatest sign of the end times — fulfilling Ezekiel literally after 2,500 years.
trad_Academic: Original context: restoration from Babylonian exile. Modern application to 1948 is theological retrospection. The passage is a hope oracle, not a calendar prediction.

keywords: kingdom|never destroyed|endure forever|crush|God of heaven|eternal|stone|four kingdoms|Nebuchadnezzar|dream
text: And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed: and the kingdom shall not be left to other people, but it shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever.
desc: The climax of Nebuchadnezzar's dream — the stone cut without hands that becomes a mountain: God's everlasting kingdom shattering the kingdoms of men.
hebrewKey: מַלְכוּ (malku) — kingdom (Aramaic); לְעָלְמִין (le-almin) — forever (Aramaic cognate of olam)
archaeology: Nebuchadnezzar's dream statue finds corroboration in the sequence: Babylon → Medo-Persia → Greece → Rome — historically confirmed by the Babylonian Chronicles and Greek/Roman records.
trad_Jewish: The eternal kingdom is the Messianic Kingdom. The stone cut without hands is the Messiah's kingdom replacing Gentile empires.
trad_Catholic: The Church is the stone kingdom, growing to fill the earth — fulfilling this now and completely at the Parousia.
trad_Protestant: Christ's kingdom established at his first coming; the stone has been rolling since Pentecost; fulfilled at the Second Coming.
trad_Dispensational: The statue represents four world empires ending with a revived Roman Empire (ten toes). The stone strikes at Christ's second coming — a yet future event.
trad_Academic: Daniel 2 is dated by critical scholars to c. 165 BC (Antiochus IV era) — making the 'prophecy' largely post-eventu. The four kingdoms are Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece, with the stone representing the Maccabean period.

text: I saw in the night visions, and, behold, one like the Son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and came to the Ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
desc: Daniel's vision of one 'like the Son of man' coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, given everlasting, universal dominion — the title Jesus took for Himself.
hebrewKey: בַּר אֱנָשׁ (bar enash) — son of man (Aramaic); the term Jesus uses of himself 80+ times in the Gospels
trad_Jewish: The 'son of man' is variously interpreted: the angel Michael (some rabbis), the nation Israel collectively (Ibn Ezra), or the future Messiah (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra).
trad_Catholic: Jesus's self-identification as the Son of Man is a deliberate claim to fulfill this vision. His ascension to the Father's right hand is the fulfillment.
trad_Protestant: The central Messianic claim — Jesus before the Sanhedrin (Matt 26:64) explicitly identifies himself with this figure. The Ascension is the fulfillment.
trad_Academic: 'Son of Man' in Daniel is a heavenly being distinct from 'one like a lion' and other beasts representing empires. The background is ANE heavenly council mythology (Canaanite El and Baal traditions).

text: And I will pour upon the house of David, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplications: and they shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourneth for his only son, and shall be in bitterness for him, as one that is in bitterness for his firstborn.
desc: Israel's national mourning when they see the one they pierced, the turning of Israel at Christ's return.
hebrewKey: וְהִבִּיטוּ אֵלַי אֵת אֲשֶׁר־דָּקָרוּ (ve-hibitu elai et asher-dakaru) — they will look to me whom they pierced
archaeology: John 19:34-37 explicitly cites this. The spear piercing is reported as eyewitness testimony.
trad_Jewish: The MT reads 'they pierced me' (God speaking) — a difficult text. Some rabbinic sources refer this to the Messiah ben Joseph who dies in battle. Others apply it to Israel being pierced by nations.
trad_Catholic: Fulfilled at the crucifixion. John's explicit citation (John 19:37) is confirmed. The pouring of the Spirit (Pentecost) is the 'spirit of grace.'
trad_Protestant: One of the most striking crucifixion prophecies — God says 'they pierced me' — supporting Christ's divinity.
trad_Oneness: YHWH says 'they pierced ME' — a key Oneness text showing YHWH himself was crucified.
trad_Dispensational: Israel's national mourning and conversion occurs at Second Coming.
trad_Academic: The MT's 'they pierced me' (אֵלַי) is textually difficult; the LXX reads 'they mocked.' The DSS (4Q254) preserves the MT reading, supporting its antiquity.

keywords: Mount of Olives|feet|split|valley|east|Jerusalem|feet stand|west|day of the LORD|living water
text: And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives, which is before Jerusalem on the east, and the mount of Olives shall cleave in the midst thereof toward the east and toward the west, and there shall be a very great valley; and half of the mountain shall remove toward the north, and half of it toward the south.
desc: Zechariah foresees the LORD's feet standing on the Mount of Olives, splitting it — the very mountain from which Christ ascended and to which angels promised His return.
hebrewKey: הַר הַזֵּיתִים (Har ha-Zeitim) — Mount of Olives; וְנִבְקַע (ve-nivka) — and it will be split/cleft
archaeology: The Mount of Olives has a geological fault running east-west. A 1927 earthquake caused significant fissures. Geologists confirm the fault line.
trad_Jewish: The Mount of Olives is the traditional site of the resurrection of the dead. The Messiah's arrival there is anticipated in Midrash Zuta (Song of Songs 2:8).
trad_Catholic: Christ ascended from the Mount of Olives; his return there is a literal expectation. The geological split is debated — possibly symbolic of cosmic upheaval.
trad_Protestant: The ascension from the same mountain points to the literal return site. Acts 1:11-12 confirms the location.
trad_Dispensational: One of the most specific topographical prophecies — the exact mountain, the direction of the split. Fulfilled literally at the Second Coming.
trad_Academic: The east-west geological fault is attested. The apocalyptic description draws on exodus traditions (sea splitting). The Mount of Olives was already associated with divine manifestation (Ezek 11:23).

text: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.
desc: The mystery of Israel's partial hardening until the Gentile fullness arrives, then all Israel saved.
hebrewKey: πᾶς Ἰσραήλ (pas Israel) — all Israel; πλήρωμα (pleroma) — fullness/full number
trad_Jewish: Paul's statement is debated in Jewish-Christian dialogue. His 'all Israel' promise is viewed by some Jewish scholars as affirming a special covenant path for Jews.
trad_Catholic: Dogmatic: a future conversion of Israel precedes the Parousia. The Catechism affirms this. The Church prays for this explicitly in the Good Friday liturgy.
trad_Protestant: A future national turning of Israel to Christ. The olive tree metaphor (Rom 11:17-24) is the foundation of covenant theology's view of Israel.
trad_Dispensational: The most explicit NT prophecy of Israel's future national salvation — fulfilled in the tribulation and at the Second Coming.
trad_Academic: Paul's 'mystery' disclosure is a key NT eschatological passage. Debate centers on whether 'all Israel' means national Israel or the full elect (Calvin). The dative 'in this way' (houtōs) is grammatically contested.

text: For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
desc: Paul's foundational description of the resurrection of dead believers and the catching-up of the living at Christ's return.
hebrewKey: ἀρχάγγελος (archaggelos) — archangel; σάλπιγξ (salpinx) — trumpet; ἁρπαγησόμεθα (harpagesometha) — we will be caught up (Lat. rapiemur → rapture)
trad_Jewish: No direct parallel — the rapture is a distinctly Christian eschatological concept, though Jewish apocalyptic has similar resurrection/ascent motifs (1 Enoch).
trad_Catholic: The resurrection of the dead at the Parousia is affirmed. The Catholic Church does not endorse a pre-tribulation rapture distinct from the Second Coming.
trad_Protestant: The general resurrection at the Second Coming. Most Reformed theologians do not distinguish rapture from the Second Coming.
trad_Dispensational: The pre-tribulation rapture — the Church is caught up before the seven-year Tribulation. The most distinctive Dispensational eschatological doctrine.
trad_Academic: Paul is comforting grieving Thessalonians, not providing a systematic eschatological timeline. The imagery draws on Jewish apocalyptic (1 Enoch, 4 Ezra) and Roman imperial parousia (royal visitation) language.

text: Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition;
desc: Paul's warning that the Day will not come until the apostasy and the revealing of the man of sin — the son of perdition who exalts himself in the temple as God.
hebrewKey: ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἀνομίας (anthropos tes anomias) — man of lawlessness; ἀποστασία (apostasia) — rebellion/apostasy
trad_Jewish: No direct parallel — the figure resembles Antiochus IV who desecrated the Temple (168 BC) and whom Daniel's 'little horn' may reference.
trad_Catholic: The Man of Lawlessness is the Antichrist of the last days. Exact identity unknown; the restrainer (v. 6-7) is debated (Holy Spirit, Roman Empire, the Church).
trad_Protestant: A future eschatological figure — the Antichrist — who will desecrate a rebuilt Jerusalem Temple.
trad_Dispensational: The Antichrist who defiles the Third Temple at the midpoint of the seven-year Tribulation — the Abomination of Desolation. Literally fulfilled.
trad_Academic: Preterist reading: Nero or Caligula (who attempted to place his statue in the Temple, AD 40). Most critical scholars see this as apocalyptic genre, not specific prediction.

text: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.
desc: Peter's declaration that the Day of the Lord will come suddenly, the present heavens and elements dissolved by fire.
hebrewKey: στοιχεῖα (stoicheia) — elements (atomic components or celestial bodies); κατακαήσεται (katakaesetai) — will be burned up/laid bare
trad_Jewish: The dissolution of the present cosmos and its renewal is found in Jewish apocalyptic (1 Enoch 72-82, 4 Ezra 7).
trad_Catholic: The final purification of creation by fire (ignis purgatorius mundi) precedes the New Creation. Not annihilation but transformation.
trad_Protestant: The present creation passes away to make way for the New Heavens and New Earth. Whether the burning is literal or metaphorical is debated.
trad_Dispensational: A literal cosmic destruction and recreation in the eternal state, following the Millennium and Great White Throne Judgment.
trad_Academic: Draws on Stoic cosmological language (ekpyrosis — world-fire). 'Elements' (stoicheia) may be celestial bodies or basic material components. The thief metaphor is shared with 1 Thessalonians 5:2.

text: And he causeth all, both small and great, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads: And that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.
desc: The second beast enforces the mark of the first beast — required to buy or sell — and the riddle of its number, 666.
hebrewKey: χάραγμα (charagma) — mark/stamp (used for imperial seals); χξς — Greek numerals for 666; νέρων (Neron) by gematria = 666
trad_Jewish: No direct OT parallel — the mark reverses the tefillin (phylacteries) worn on hand and forehead. Antithetical to God's mark on his people.
trad_Catholic: The Mark is a future end-times allegiance to the Antichrist. The Church warns against any economic system that requires rejection of God.
trad_Protestant: A literal end-times mark — possibly a technology enabling totalitarian economic control. The 666 is a human number, contrasted with 777 (divine perfection).
trad_Dispensational: A literal physical mark in the Great Tribulation — possibly microchip, biometric scan, or tattoo — enabling global economic control by the Beast.
trad_Academic: Preterist: 666 is Nero Caesar by Hebrew/Greek gematria — widely accepted by scholars (Collins, Aune). The mark satirizes Roman imperial seals and commerce. Revelation's genre is Jewish apocalyptic, not future prediction.

text: And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them: and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.
desc: John sees the martyrs raised to reign with Christ for a thousand years — the central text of the millennium debate.
hebrewKey: χίλια ἔτη (chilia ete) — thousand years; ἔζησαν (ezesan) — they came to life (first resurrection)
trad_Jewish: No direct parallel — but the Messianic Kingdom of 1,000 years appears in some Jewish apocalyptic texts (2 Baruch 40:3, 4 Ezra 7:28).
trad_Catholic: Amillennial: the thousand years is the current Church age. Martyrs reign with Christ spiritually now. Awaits the single Parousia.
trad_Protestant: Divided: amillennial (symbolic 1000 years, current age), premillennial (literal future 1000-year kingdom after Christ's return), postmillennial (gospel age of triumph).
trad_Dispensational: A literal 1,000-year reign of Christ on earth from Jerusalem after his Second Coming and binding of Satan. The most detailed end-times expectation.
trad_Academic: The 1,000-year figure is symbolic (cf. Psalm 50:10, 2 Pet 3:8). The 'first resurrection' is debated — bodily or spiritual? Revelation's imagery draws on Daniel 7:9-27.

text: In that day shall there be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar at the border thereof to the LORD. And it shall be for a sign and for a witness unto the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt: for they shall cry unto the LORD because of the oppressors, and he shall send them a saviour, and a great one, and he shall deliver them.
desc: A future altar and pillar to the LORD in Egypt, pointing to Egypt's eschatological inclusion in God's people.
hebrewKey: מִזְבֵּחַ לַיהוָה (mizbeach la-YHWH) — altar to YHWH; מַצֵּבָה (matsevah) — pillar/monument
archaeology: The Jewish Temple at Elephantine (5th c. BC, Aswan area) was a Jewish temple on Egypt's border. The Leontopolis temple (c. 160 BC, Tell el-Yahudiyya) was built by Onias IV with priestly approval.
trad_Jewish: The Elephantine and Leontopolis temples may fulfill this. The text also points to Egypt's eschatological turning to God.
trad_Catholic: The early Christian community in Alexandria is the fulfillment — Egypt became one of the earliest and most vibrant centers of Christianity.
trad_Protestant: Partial historical fulfillment (Elephantine/Leontopolis); full eschatological fulfillment when Egypt turns to God.
trad_Academic: The Elephantine Jewish temple (destroyed 410 BC) and Leontopolis temple (30 BC–73 AD) are the strongest historical candidates. The Egyptian Jewish diaspora is well-documented archaeologically.

text: The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground?
desc: Edom's destruction despite their clifftop stronghold Petra, fulfilled in their historical annihilation.
hebrewKey: שֶׁלַּע (sela') — rock/Petra; גֵּאֹון לִבְּךָ (ge'on libbecha) — pride of your heart
archaeology: Petra (Sela in Hebrew) — the rose-red city carved in the sandstone cliffs of Edom — was abandoned after Arab conquests. Modern excavations (Brown University Petra Archaeological Project) confirm the ancient city. Edom as a distinct people ceased to exist after the 1st century AD.
trad_Jewish: Edom is frequently identified in rabbinic literature with Rome, and its judgment with Rome's eventual fall.
trad_Catholic: Fulfilled historically — Edom was absorbed by the Nabataeans, then by Rome. The proud cliff-dwellers were humbled.
trad_Protestant: A model of literal prophetic fulfillment — Edom/Petra is desolate exactly as predicted.
trad_Academic: Edomite civilization is well-attested archaeologically. Petra's abandonment is historically confirmed. Whether the abandonment fulfills Obadiah or results from normal historical processes is interpretive.

text: Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
desc: Jonah's three days in the fish, cited by Jesus as the sign of the Son of Man's three days in the earth.
hebrewKey: שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה לֵילוֹת (shloshah yamim u-shloshah leilot) — three days and three nights
trad_Jewish: The story of Jonah is read on Yom Kippur — the day of repentance — because Nineveh's repentance is central. The fish episode is typological in Jewish interpretation.
trad_Catholic: Jesus identifies this as the 'sign of Jonah' — the Son of Man's death and resurrection. Patristic consensus from Origen onward.
trad_Protestant: The primary type of the resurrection — three days in the 'heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40). The most important typological sign Jesus gave.
trad_Academic: Jonah is generally classified as a didactic narrative (parable/novella) rather than strict history by critical scholars. The sign of Jonah as resurrection typology is Jesus's own hermeneutic.

text: For the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house.
desc: Division within families as a sign of the times, quoted by Jesus as a consequence of his coming.
hebrewKey: אֹיְבֵי אִישׁ אַנְשֵׁי בֵיתוֹ (oyevei ish anshei veito) — a man's enemies are men of his house
trad_Jewish: A description of social breakdown in the Assyrian crisis — the collapse of covenant loyalty at every level of society.
trad_Catholic: Jesus quotes this directly (Matt 10:35-36) to describe the divisions his mission creates. The gospel divides families before it restores them.
trad_Protestant: Christ's citation makes this directly applicable to his mission — the gospel creates conflict before peace.
trad_Academic: Micah 7:1-7 is a lament over social disintegration. Jesus cites it to describe the social impact of his movement — which historically did divide families across ethnic and religious lines.

text: And the Gentiles shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising.
desc: Gentile kings and nations drawn to Israel's light, fulfilled in the Magi and the spread of the gospel to all nations.
hebrewKey: גּוֹיִם (goyim) — nations/Gentiles; אוֹרֵךְ (orech) — your light; נָגְהֶךָ (nogheha) — your brightness
archaeology: The Magi visit (Matt 2) is set in the broader context of Isaiah 60's vision of Gentile kings bringing gifts.
trad_Jewish: The eschatological ingathering of Gentile nations to Jerusalem. One of the most cherished restoration oracles.
trad_Catholic: The Magi (Matt 2) are the first Gentile 'kings' coming to the light of Christ — an early fulfillment. The Revelation 21:24 is eschatological.
trad_Protestant: Being fulfilled through the global expansion of Christianity; fully consummated in the New Jerusalem.
trad_Dispensational: Millennial fulfillment — Gentile nations literally come to Jerusalem to worship during the 1,000-year reign of Christ.
trad_Academic: Isaiah 60 is one of the great restoration poems. The Magi narrative in Matthew may consciously allude to it. Revelation 21:24 is a direct citation.

text: Thus saith the LORD; A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not.
desc: Rachel weeping for her children, cited by Matthew as fulfilled in Herod's massacre of the Bethlehem infants.
hebrewKey: קוֹל בְּרָמָה נִשְׁמַע (kol be-Ramah nishma) — a voice in Ramah is heard; רָחֵל (Rachel) — ancestral mother of Joseph/Benjamin tribes
archaeology: Ramah (er-Ram) is 5 miles north of Jerusalem. The massacre of Bethlehem's infants is reported only by Matthew.
trad_Jewish: Original context: Jeremiah envisions the exiles passing through Ramah (near Bethlehem) on the way to Babylon. Rachel weeps for her descendants going into exile.
trad_Catholic: Matthew's fulfillment is typological — the massacre of the innocents recapitulates Israel's exile tragedy. Matthew sees Christ reliving Israel's history.
trad_Protestant: Matthew's pesher application — the pattern of Rachel's mourning is fulfilled in Herod's massacre.
trad_Academic: Matthew's use is a classic pesher — the original text is about the Babylonian exile, not prediction of Herod. Matthew identifies patterns, not literal forecasts. The historicity of the massacre is debated by scholars.

text: And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
desc: The second regathering of Israel from the four corners of the earth, fulfilled progressively from 1948 onward.
hebrewKey: כָּנְפוֹת הָאָרֶץ (kanfot ha-aretz) — four corners/wings of the earth; נִדְחֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (nidchei Yisrael) — dispersed of Israel
archaeology: Modern aliyah from 100+ nations — USSR (1990s), Ethiopia (Operation Moses/Solomon), Yemen, North America, Europe — is documented by the Jewish Agency.
trad_Jewish: One of the central Messianic redemption texts. The ingathering of exiles (Kibbutz Galuyot) is a foundational principle of Jewish Messianic hope.
trad_Catholic: Partially fulfilled in the post-exilic return; eschatologically in the final ingathering at the Parousia.
trad_Protestant: Being fulfilled in modern aliyah — a remarkable modern sign; fully consummated at the Second Coming.
trad_Dispensational: The most important sign of the end times — the regathering of Israel from all nations precisely fulfills this.
trad_Academic: Original context: Assyrian exile. Applied to 1948 is theological retrospection. The fourfold direction is a merism for totality (all directions).

text: For I will take you from among the heathen, and gather you out of all countries, and will bring you into your own land.
desc: God's promise to regather Israel from all countries to their land, fulfilled in the Zionist return and 1948 statehood.
hebrewKey: וְלָקַחְתִּי אֶתְכֶם מִן־הַגּוֹיִם (ve-lakachti etchem min-ha-goyim) — I will take you from the nations
archaeology: The Jewish Agency documents aliyah from 100+ countries since 1882. The State of Israel absorbed 3+ million immigrants from the Soviet Union, Ethiopia, Yemen, and elsewhere.
trad_Jewish: Central to modern Religious Zionist theology (Rav Kook). The secular Zionist movement unconsciously fulfills the prophecy of physical return.
trad_Catholic: The post-exilic return and the modern state both partially fulfill this. Full fulfillment awaits the Messianic era.
trad_Protestant: The modern State of Israel is a fulfillment. God is regathering his people for the eschatological drama.
trad_Dispensational: One of the clearest modern fulfillments — Israel in the land is the clock of prophecy. The generation of 1948 is the 'fig tree' generation.
trad_Academic: Original context is the Babylonian exile. The spiritual transformation (36:25-27) is the heart of the oracle — the physical return is secondary to the new covenant promise.

text: Son of man, set thy face against Gog, the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and prophesy against him … After many days thou shalt be visited: in the latter years thou shalt come into the land that is brought back from the sword, and is gathered out of many people, against the mountains of Israel, which have been always waste … I will go up to the land of unwalled villages; I will go to them that are at rest, that dwell safely … To take a spoil, and to take a prey; to turn thine hand upon the desolate places that are now inhabited
desc: The opening of the Gog oracle — God sets His face against Gog of Magog, the great northern coalition that comes against restored Israel and is destroyed.
hebrewKey: גּוֹג (Gog) — possibly a title or name; אֶרֶץ הַמָּגוֹג (eretz ha-Magog) — land of Magog; רֹאשׁ (rosh) — chief/head
archaeology: Magog, Meshek (Mushki), and Tubal are attested in Assyrian records and in Genesis 10 (Table of Nations). The Assyrian Annals of Tiglath-Pileser III mention Tubal and Meshek as Anatolian kingdoms.
trad_Jewish: An eschatological coalition attacking Israel before the Messianic age. Gog/Magog is the climactic final battle in Jewish apocalyptic (Talmud Sanhedrin 97b).
trad_Catholic: An eschatological figure of evil attacking God's people. May refer to events before or after the Millennium.
trad_Protestant: A future confederacy of northern nations (Russia, Turkey, Iran, Libya) attacking Israel in the last days.
trad_Dispensational: Russia (Rosh = Russia) leading a coalition (Iran, Turkey, Libya, Sudan) against Israel during the Tribulation. One of the most specifically identified future prophecies.
trad_Academic: Gog is likely a symbolic/composite figure. Magog is associated with Anatolia or Scythia. Critical scholars see this as apocalyptic literature, not a strategic forecast. Revelation 20:8 uses it symbolically.

text: But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
desc: The Suffering Servant bearing vicarious wounds for our transgressions, the heart of substitutionary atonement.
hebrewKey: מְחֹלָל (mecholal) — pierced; דַּכָּא (daka) — crushed; בַּחֲבֻרָתוֹ (ba-chavurato) — by his wound/stripe
archaeology: The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa^a, Dead Sea Scrolls, c. 125 BC) preserves this text virtually identical to the MT, proving the text predates Christ by over a century.
trad_Jewish: The dominant rabbinic interpretation is corporate Israel as the suffering servant — Israel suffers among the nations to bring light to the world. Rashi, Maimonides, and Ibn Ezra favor this reading.
trad_Catholic: The Servant is Christ — this is the most cited OT passage in the NT regarding the Atonement. The passion narrative is saturated with Isaiah 53 allusions.
trad_Protestant: The supreme OT prophecy of substitutionary atonement — Christ bears our sins. Calvin called it the fifth Gospel.
trad_Academic: Isaiah 53 is the most debated OT chapter. The identity of the Servant (individual, collective, or royal) is contested. The DSS text (1QIsa^a) proves the pre-Christian origin of the text.

text: And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.
desc: The Servant's grave with the wicked (crucified between criminals) and burial with the rich (Joseph of Arimathea's tomb).
hebrewKey: עִם־עָשִׁיר בְּמֹתָיו (im-ashir be-motav) — with the rich in his death; the contrast between 'wicked grave' (crucifixion context) and 'rich man's tomb' is striking
archaeology: The tomb of Joseph of Arimathea (a 'prominent member of the Council', Mark 15:43) is consistent with rock-cut tombs of wealthy 1st-century Jews in Jerusalem. Garden Tomb and Church of Holy Sepulchre are the two candidate sites.
trad_Jewish: The corporate servant interpretation sees Israel buried among the nations (wicked) yet preserved. The contrast between wicked burial and honorable interment is allegorical.
trad_Catholic: Precisely fulfilled — executed with criminals (wicked grave) yet buried by Joseph of Arimathea (rich man). An unlikely juxtaposition the evangelists highlight.
trad_Protestant: One of the most specific Servant Song details — the rich tomb is improbable for an executed criminal and stands out as fulfilled prophecy.
trad_Academic: The Joseph of Arimathea burial is one of the most historically discussed elements of the passion narrative. John Dominic Crossan questions it; N.T. Wright and others defend its historicity.

text: For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
desc: David's psalm of confidence in resurrection, cited by Peter and Paul as a prophecy of Christ's resurrection.
hebrewKey: שְׁאוֹל (sheol) — realm of the dead; שַׁחַת (shachat) — pit/decay; חָסִיד (chasid) — faithful/godly one
archaeology: Peter's Pentecost sermon (Acts 2) and Paul at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13) both cite this Psalm as proven fulfilled by Christ's resurrection — the earliest Christian preaching.
trad_Jewish: David speaks of his own confidence in God's protection from premature death. The 'faithful one' is David. Traditional Jewish reading is personal — God's protection for the righteous.
trad_Catholic: Peter's Pentecost argument (Acts 2:29): David died and his tomb is known, therefore David spoke of another — Christ — whose body did not decay.
trad_Protestant: The two NT citations (Acts 2, 13) lock in the resurrection fulfillment. David could not say this of himself — he is the prophet.
trad_Oneness: Specifically foretells the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
trad_Academic: The Psalmic application of 'no decay' to resurrection is a distinctive Christian hermeneutic. Peter's argument (David's tomb is here) is an early example of NT pesher on burial customs.

text: Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
desc: The betrayal by a close friend at table, cited by Jesus as fulfilled in Judas who ate with him.
hebrewKey: אִישׁ שְׁלוֹמִי (ish shelomi) — man of my peace/close friend; אֲשֶׁר־אָכַל לַחְמִי (asher achal lachmi) — who ate my bread
trad_Jewish: David speaks of Ahithophel — his trusted counselor who betrayed him for Absalom (2 Sam 15-17). Ahithophel then hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23).
trad_Catholic: Jesus explicitly applies this to Judas at the Last Supper (John 13:18). The bread-sharing at the Passover Seder makes the betrayal all the more poignant.
trad_Protestant: A typological fulfillment — David's betrayal by Ahithophel prefigures Christ's betrayal by Judas, who also hanged himself (Matt 27:5).
trad_Academic: The parallel David/Judas and Ahithophel structure is noted by scholars. Jesus's self-application in John 13 is explicit. Whether Psalm 41 is 'predictive' or a pattern is interpretive.

text: I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles;
desc: The Servant as covenant for the people and light for the Gentiles, opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners.
hebrewKey: בְּרִית עָם (berit am) — covenant of the people; אוֹר גּוֹיִם (or goyim) — light of the Gentiles; עוּוֵר (iver) — blind
trad_Jewish: The Servant is Israel — called to be a light to the nations (cf. Gen 12:3). The blind and captive are both Israel in exile and Gentiles in ignorance.
trad_Catholic: Simeon's canticle (Luke 2:32) directly applies this to Jesus — 'a light for revelation to the Gentiles.' The Servant's mission is fulfilled in Christ and extended through the Church.
trad_Protestant: Christ is the Servant who fulfills this — his healing of the blind is both literal and symbolic. Paul cites 42:6 in Acts 13:47 as authorizing the Gentile mission.
trad_Academic: The first of the four Servant Songs (42:1-9). Whether the Servant is Israel, an individual (pre-exilic prophet, Cyrus) or Messianic is the central hermeneutical question of Isaiah 40-55.

text: And he said unto Abram, Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years;
desc: The 400-year Egyptian bondage predicted to Abraham, fulfilled exactly in the Exodus.
hebrewKey: גֵּר יִהְיֶה זַרְעֲךָ (ger yihyeh zar'acha) — your seed will be a sojourner; אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה (arba me'ot shanah) — 400 years
archaeology: The Ipuwer Papyrus (Leiden Museum) may reflect Egyptian turmoil associated with the Exodus. Brickmaking records from Deir el-Medina and the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC) provide context.
trad_Jewish: Fulfilled in the Exodus — the Passover is the memorial celebration of this fulfillment. The 400-year figure is discussed in the Talmud (Seder Olam).
trad_Catholic: God's covenant faithfulness demonstrated — he predicted and then fulfilled the Egyptian sojourn and Exodus. A prefiguring of baptism.
trad_Protestant: A model of predictive covenant fulfillment — 400 years before the Exodus. Demonstrates God's sovereign foreknowledge.
trad_Academic: The 400/430-year figures present harmonization challenges (Gen 15:13 vs Exod 12:40). The historical Exodus date is debated (15th c. vs 13th c. BC). The Merneptah Stele places Israel in Canaan by 1208 BC.

text: God brought him forth out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn: he shall eat up the nations his enemies, and shall break their bones, and pierce them through with his arrows.
desc: Balaam's oracle of Israel coming out of Egypt with divine strength, consuming their enemies.
hebrewKey: תּוֹעֲפֹת רְאֵם לוֹ (to'afot re'em lo) — he has the strength of a wild ox; רְאֵם (re'em) — wild ox (aurochs)
archaeology: The conquest of Canaan is archaeologically complex. Jericho (Tell es-Sultan) shows Late Bronze Age destruction. Hazor (Tell Hazor) has a destruction layer c. 1200 BC confirmed by Amnon Ben-Tor.
trad_Jewish: Balaam's blessing — a Gentile prophet compelled to bless Israel. Fulfilled in the conquest of Canaan and subsequent victories.
trad_Catholic: God's strength given to Israel is a type of the Church's spiritual warfare and victory through Christ.
trad_Protestant: Fulfilled in the conquest of Canaan — the military victories of Joshua demonstrate God's fulfillment of Balaam's oracle.
trad_Dispensational: Literal conquest of hostile nations in the Millennial Kingdom.
trad_Academic: Balaam is attested extrabiblically — the Deir Alla inscription (c. 800 BC) mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor, consistent with Numbers 22-24. A remarkable extrabiblical confirmation.

fulfillmentRefs: Luke 21:24|Romans 11:25|AD 70 Roman dispersion|2,000 years of Jewish Diaspora
text: And the LORD shall scatter thee among all people, from the one end of the earth even unto the other; and there thou shalt serve other gods, which neither thou nor thy fathers have known, even wood and stone.
desc: The Diaspora scattering of Israel to the ends of the earth as covenant curse, fulfilled throughout history.
hebrewKey: וֶהֱפִיצְךָ יְהוָה בְּכָל־הָעַמִּים (ve-hefitzcha YHWH be-chol-ha-ammim) — YHWH will scatter you among all peoples
archaeology: Jewish communities (diaspora) are archaeologically attested from Spain to India from the 1st century AD. Synagogue remains are found across the Roman Empire, Persia, Egypt, and Arabia.
trad_Jewish: Fulfilled in the two dispersions — Assyrian (722 BC) and Babylonian/Roman (586 BC and AD 70). The diaspora is the painful backdrop of all Jewish history.
trad_Catholic: Moses' warning is a historical fact. The dispersion pointed forward to the Church's universal mission — and back to Israel's covenant unfaithfulness.
trad_Protestant: One of the most precisely fulfilled prophecies — the Jewish people have been scattered to every nation exactly as predicted.
trad_Dispensational: The dispersion is ended by the modern regathering to Israel — the fulfillment of both halves of this covenant (scattering and return).
trad_Academic: Deuteronomy 28's blessings and curses are standard ANE treaty/covenant formulae (cf. Esarhaddon's vassal treaties). The historical accuracy of the dispersion is undeniable. Whether Moses predicted it or it was written post-eventu is the critical question.

text: And I will scatter you among the heathen, and will draw out a sword after you: and your land shall be desolate, and your cities waste.
desc: The covenant curse of scattering among the nations with land desolation, fulfilled in 70 AD and the Roman wars.
hebrewKey: וַהֲשִׁמֹּתִי אֲנִי אֶת־הָאָרֶץ (va-hashimoti ani et-ha-aretz) — I will devastate the land; עָרֵיכֶם יִהְיוּ חָרְבָּה (areichem yihyu charvah) — your cities will be ruins
archaeology: Roman destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70) is documented by Josephus, the Arch of Titus (Rome, AD 81), and extensive excavation. The Israel Antiquities Authority documents the burnt layer from AD 70 in the City of David.
trad_Jewish: Fulfilled twice — by Babylon (586 BC) and Rome (AD 70). The desolation of the land is a central theological problem in post-destruction rabbinic theology.
trad_Catholic: The destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70) is fulfillment of both Moses and Jesus (Luke 21:24). The land's restoration in modern times is a further fulfillment.
trad_Protestant: A historically precise fulfillment — the land was desolate for 1,878 years before the modern Jewish return.
trad_Dispensational: The desolation and restoration are both fulfilled — one of the most remarkable long-range prophecies in Scripture.
trad_Academic: The historical desolation of Judea under Roman rule is exceptionally well-documented. Mark Twain (1867) described a barren, nearly uninhabited land. The agricultural recovery post-1880 is equally well documented.

text: I will raise them up a Prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him.
desc: Moses predicting a Prophet like himself from Israel's midst, applied to Jesus by Peter, Stephen, and Philip.
hebrewKey: נָבִיא אָקִים לָהֶם מִקֶּרֶב אֲחֵיהֶם כָּמוֹךָ (navi akum lahem mi-kerev acheihem kamokha) — I will raise up a prophet like you from among their brothers
trad_Jewish: The expectation of a prophet 'like Moses' was alive in Second Temple Judaism — the Qumran community expected an Eschatological Prophet alongside the Priestly and Royal Messiahs (1QS 9:11). The Samaritan woman (John 4) and the crowds (John 6:14) both identify Jesus as 'the Prophet.'
trad_Catholic: Fulfilled in Christ — the ultimate prophet, priest, and king. Peter (Acts 3:22) and Stephen (Acts 7:37) explicitly apply this to Jesus.
trad_Protestant: The Prophet like Moses is Jesus — who mediates a new covenant, performs exodus signs, and speaks God's words directly.
trad_Academic: The expectation of an Eschatological Moses figure is well-attested in DSS (4QTestimonia, 4Q175) and in Samaritan theology. The Qumran tripartite Messianism (Prophet, Priest, King) illuminates the NT's Christological claims.

text: And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
desc: The Spirit of God hovering over creation, prefiguring the Spirit's role in the new creation at Pentecost.

text: But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.
desc: Death entering humanity through disobedience, the curse Christ reversed through his obedience unto death.

text: And the LORD God said unto the serpent, Because thou hast done this, thou art cursed above all cattle, and above every beast of the field; upon thy belly shalt thou go, and dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life:
desc: The curse on the serpent and the enmity established between the seed of the serpent and the seed of the woman.

text: Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.
desc: Pain in childbirth and marital tension as consequence of the Fall, realities reversed in Christ's redemption.

text: And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;
desc: Human mortality and labor as consequences of sin, overcome in Christ's resurrection and the coming new creation.

text: And now art thou cursed from the earth, which hath opened her mouth to receive thy brother's blood from thy hand; When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be in the earth.
desc: Cain cursed to be a wandering fugitive, a type of spiritual exile from God's presence due to sin.

text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.
desc: God limiting human lifespan and setting a deadline before judgment, fulfilled in the Flood after 120 years.

text: And God said unto Noah, The end of all flesh is come before me; for the earth is filled with violence through them; and, behold, I will destroy them with the earth.
desc: God's announcement of the Flood as judgment on universal corruption, with Noah preserved as a type of salvation.

text: For yet seven days, and I will cause it to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights; and every living substance that I have made will I destroy from off the face of the earth.
desc: The precise prediction of the Flood's beginning, fulfilled exactly seven days later.

sub: The Noahic pledge of the seasons
text: And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake; for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done.
desc: God's pledge after the Flood — never again to destroy all life by flood, and the unfailing rhythm of the seasons while the earth endures.

text: And I will establish my covenant with you; neither shall all flesh be cut off any more by the waters of a flood; neither shall there any more be a flood to destroy the earth.
desc: God's promise never to destroy the earth again by flood, sealed with the rainbow covenant.

sub: The LORD God of Shem; Japheth in his tents
text: And he said, Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren. And he said, Blessed be the LORD God of Shem; and Canaan shall be his servant.
desc: Noah's prophetic blessing — the LORD identified as 'the God of Shem,' through whose line salvation comes, with Japheth (the Gentiles) dwelling in Shem's tents.

text: And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
desc: The scattering of humanity and confusion of languages at Babel, fulfilled immediately and reversed at Pentecost.

text: And the LORD appeared unto Abram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him.
desc: The original land promise to Abraham's descendants, progressively fulfilled through Israel's history.

text: And the LORD said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:
desc: God confirming the land promise to Abraham after Lot's departure, covering all of Canaan.

text: And blessed be the most high God, which hath delivered thine enemies into thy hand. And he gave him tithes of all.
desc: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High, blessing Abram with bread and wine — the priest-king type fulfilled in Christ (Psalm 110; Hebrews 7).

sub: From the river of Egypt to the Euphrates
text: In the same day the LORD made a covenant with Abram, saying, Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates:
desc: God's formal covenant granting Abraham's seed the land from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates — the foundational land-promise of Israel.

text: And the angel of the LORD said unto her, I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude. And the angel of the LORD said unto her, Behold, thou art with child, and shalt bear a son, and shalt call his name Ishmael; because the LORD hath heard thy affliction.
desc: God's promise to multiply Hagar's descendants into a great nation, fulfilled in the Arab peoples.

text: And he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren.
desc: Ishmael's descendants predicted as perennial warriors in conflict with their neighbors, fulfilled in Arab history.

text: As for me, behold, my covenant is with thee, and thou shalt be a father of many nations. Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee.
desc: God's covenant with Abraham — father of many nations, with kings in his line — fulfilled in the multitude of believing nations and the King, Christ.

text: And I will give unto thee, and to thy seed after thee, the land wherein thou art a stranger, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession; and I will be their God.
desc: The everlasting land covenant with Abraham, ultimately pointing to the eternal inheritance in the new creation.

text: And I will bless her, and give thee a son also of her: yea, I will bless her, and she shall be a mother of nations; kings of people shall be of her.
desc: The miraculous birth of Isaac to aged Sarah predicted, fulfilled and serving as a type of the virgin birth.

text: And as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly; twelve princes shall he beget, and I will make him a great nation.
desc: God's promise to multiply Ishmael into a great nation, fulfilled in the twelve princes of Ishmael.

text: Seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?
desc: The universal blessing to all nations through Abraham's seed, ultimately fulfilled in Christ the promised descendant.

text: And God said unto Abraham, Let it not be grievous in thy sight because of the lad, and because of thy bondwoman; in all that Sarah hath said unto thee, hearken unto her voice; for in Isaac shall thy seed be called.
desc: God's word that Abraham's covenant seed would be reckoned through Isaac — applied by Paul to the children of promise and by Hebrews to the resurrection hope.

text: And also of the son of the bondwoman will I make a nation, because he is thy seed.
desc: Ishmael promised to become a great nation though not the covenant heir, fulfilled in the Arab peoples.

sub: The Seed who blesses the nations
text: That in blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore; and thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies;
desc: The climactic Abrahamic promise — in Abraham's Seed all nations blessed — which Paul reads as singular, fulfilled in the one Seed, Christ.

text: And the LORD said unto her, Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.
desc: The LORD's oracle to Rebekah — two nations (Israel and Edom) in her womb, the elder to serve the younger — which Paul cites on divine election (Rom. 9:12).

text: Sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee, and will bless thee; for unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give all these countries, and I will perform the oath which I sware unto Abraham thy father;
desc: God confirming to Isaac the Abrahamic promises of land and seed at Gerar.

text: And the LORD appeared unto him the same night, and said, I am the God of Abraham thy father: fear not, for I am with thee, and will bless thee, and multiply thy seed for my servant Abraham's sake.
desc: God reaffirming the Abrahamic covenant to Isaac at Beer-sheba, ensuring the promise continues through the chosen line.

text: And he came near, and kissed him: and he smelled the smell of his raiment, and blessed him, and said, See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed:
desc: Isaac's prophetic blessing on Jacob — fruitfulness, dominion over nations and brethren, echoing the Abrahamic 'bless those who bless you.'

text: And Isaac his father answered and said unto him, Behold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above; And by thy sword shalt thou live, and shalt serve thy brother; and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck.
desc: Isaac's word over Esau — Edom living by the sword, serving Jacob, yet later breaking his yoke — fulfilled in the turbulent history of Edom and Israel.

sub: The ladder joining heaven and earth
text: And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth, and thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south: and in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed.
desc: God's renewal of the seed-promise to Jacob at Bethel, where the ladder joined heaven and earth — a scene Jesus applies to Himself (John 1:51).

text: And God said unto him, I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins;
desc: God Almighty's covenant word to Jacob — a company of nations and kings from his line — the royal seed leading to the Messiah-King.

sub: The sheaves and the stars bow
text: For, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves stood round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.
desc: Joseph's two dreams — the sheaves and the sun, moon, and stars bowing — foretelling his rise and his family's submission, fulfilled when his brothers bowed in Egypt.

text: And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.
desc: God's presence with Joseph despite slavery and imprisonment, ensuring his rise to power as a type of Christ exalted.

text: Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thine head, and restore thee unto thy place: and thou shalt deliver Pharaoh's cup into his hand, after the former manner when thou wast his butler.
desc: Joseph's prediction of the cupbearer's restoration in three days, fulfilled exactly, foreshadowing resurrection.

text: Yet within three days shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee, and shall hang thee on a tree; and the birds shall eat thy flesh from off thee.
desc: Joseph's prediction of the baker's execution in three days, fulfilled exactly as predicted.

sub: Seven years of plenty, seven of famine
text: And Joseph said unto Pharaoh, The dream of Pharaoh is one: God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do. The seven good kine are seven years; and the seven good ears are seven years: the dream is one.
desc: Joseph's God-given interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams — seven years of plenty then seven of famine — fulfilled exactly, saving Egypt and the nations.

text: And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
desc: Joseph's famine prediction fulfilled exactly, with only Egypt prepared through Joseph's God-given plan.

text: And he said, I am God, the God of thy father: fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation:
desc: God's promise to Jacob that Israel would become a great nation in Egypt, fulfilled over 400 years.

text: And said unto me, Behold, I will make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, and I will make of thee a multitude of people; and will give this land to thy seed after thee for an everlasting possession.
desc: God confirming to Jacob at Bethel that the land promised to Abraham would belong to his descendants forever.

sub: The younger greater; a multitude of nations
text: And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim's head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh's head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.
desc: Jacob, crossing his hands, sets the younger Ephraim above Manasseh and foretells his seed becoming a multitude of nations — fulfilled in Ephraim's later prominence.

text: Reuben, thou art my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, the excellency of dignity, and the excellency of power: Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed; then defiledst thou it: he went up to my couch.
desc: Reuben losing his birthright due to instability and moral failure, fulfilled as the tribe never produced a judge, king, or prophet.

text: Simeon and Levi are brethren; instruments of cruelty are in their habitations. O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united: for in their anger they slew a man, and in their selfwill they digged down a wall.
desc: Simeon and Levi cursed to be scattered in Israel for the Shechem massacre, Simeon absorbed into Judah, Levi dispersed as priests.

sub: The colt, the vine, the blood of grapes
text: Binding his foal unto the vine, and his ass's colt unto the choice vine; he washed his garments in wine, and his clothes in the blood of grapes: His eyes shall be red with wine, and his teeth white with milk.
desc: The close of Jacob's blessing on Judah — abundance of wine and the colt — read messianically of the coming Ruler (with Judah's scepter, 49:10).

text: Zebulun shall dwell at the haven of the sea; and he shall be for an haven of ships; and his border shall be unto Zidon.
desc: Zebulun's tribal territory along the northern sea routes, fulfilled in the tribe's coastal Galilean settlement.

text: Issachar is a strong ass couching down between two burdens: And he saw that rest was good, and the land that it was pleasant; and bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant unto tribute.
desc: Issachar's tribe predicted as hard-working and content with agricultural labor, fulfilled in their settled fertile territory.

text: Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel. Dan shall be a serpent by the way, an adder in the path, that biteth the horse heels, so that his rider shall fall backward.
desc: Dan fulfilling a judging role but through treachery, fulfilled in Samson from Dan and the tribe's idolatry at Laish.

text: Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last.
desc: Gad's tribe prone to attack but ultimately victorious, fulfilled in their fierce military history east of Jordan.

text: Out of Asher his bread shall be fat, and he shall yield royal dainties.
desc: Asher's territory producing rich agricultural abundance fit for royalty, fulfilled in the fertile coastal plain of Asher.

text: Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words.
desc: Naphtali's swift and eloquent character, fulfilled in the region that became the heartland of Jesus's Galilean ministry.

text: Joseph is a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall: The archers have sorely grieved him, and shot at him, and hated him:
desc: Joseph's tribe (Ephraim and Manasseh) predicted to be abundantly fruitful and to extend beyond borders.

text: Benjamin shall ravin as a wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and at night he shall divide the spoil.
desc: Benjamin predicted as fierce warriors, fulfilled in Saul, Jonathan, and Paul, all Benjaminites known for fighting prowess.

text: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them; every one according to his blessing he blessed them.
desc: Jacob's final blessings over all twelve sons prophetically outlining each tribe's future character and territory.

text: And he said, Certainly I will be with thee; and this shall be a token unto thee, that I have sent thee: When thou hast brought forth the people out of Egypt, ye shall serve God upon this mountain.
desc: God promising Moses that Israel would worship on Sinai after the Exodus, fulfilled when Israel camped at Horeb.

sub: Israel shall not go out empty
text: And I will give this people favour in the sight of the Egyptians: and it shall come to pass, that, when ye go, ye shall not go empty: But every woman shall borrow of her neighbour, and of her that sojourneth in her house, jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment: and ye shall put them upon your sons, and upon your daughters; and ye shall spoil the Egyptians.
desc: God's word that Israel would leave Egypt not empty-handed but laden with its wealth — fulfilled at the Exodus, as foretold to Abraham (Gen. 15:14).

text: And it shall come to pass, if they will not believe thee, neither hearken to the voice of the first sign, that they will believe the voice of the latter sign. And it shall come to pass, if they will not believe also these two signs, neither hearken unto thy voice, that thou shalt take of the water of the river, and pour it upon the dry land: and the water which thou takest out of the river shall become blood upon the dry land.
desc: God predicting the signs needed to convince Egypt, fulfilled through the ten plagues and miraculous works.

sub: I will bring you out, redeem you, take you, bring you in
text: Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:
desc: God's sevenfold 'I will' promise of redemption — to bring Israel out, redeem them, take them as His people, and bring them into the land — the Exodus foretold.

text: And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt. But Pharaoh shall not hearken unto you, that I may lay my hand upon Egypt, and bring forth mine armies, and my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great judgments.
desc: God foretells the hardening of Pharaoh, the multiplied signs, and that Egypt will know the LORD when He delivers Israel — fulfilled through the plagues and the Exodus.

text: And I will sever in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there; to the end thou mayest know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
desc: God distinguishing Israel from Egypt in the plagues, the swarm plague passing over Goshen exactly as predicted.

text: And the LORD appointed a set time, saying, To morrow the LORD shall do this thing in the land. And the LORD did that thing on the morrow, and all the cattle of Egypt died: but of the cattle of the children of Israel died not one.
desc: God setting an exact time for the plague on Egypt's livestock, fulfilled the next day with only Egyptian animals dying.

text: For I will at this time send all my plagues upon thine heart, and upon thy servants, and upon thy people; that thou mayest know that there is none like me in all the earth.
desc: God declaring his purpose to display unparalleled power through the plagues, that Egypt would acknowledge his uniqueness.

text: Behold, to morrow about this time I will cause it to rain a very grievous hail, such as hath not been in Egypt since the foundation thereof even until now.
desc: God predicting an unprecedented hailstorm exactly on schedule, fulfilled the next day devastating Egyptian crops.

text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Stretch out thine hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt. And Moses stretched forth his hand toward heaven; and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days:
desc: The death of Egypt's firstborn predicted at midnight, the final plague fulfilled with precise timing.

text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Yet will I bring one plague more upon Pharaoh, and upon Egypt; afterwards he will let you go hence: when he shall let you go, he shall surely thrust you out hence altogether.
desc: God predicting the final plague would break Pharaoh's will and release Israel, fulfilled in the Passover night.

sub: The blood that spares from death
text: For I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD.
desc: The Passover: the blood of the lamb on the doorposts sparing the firstborn — the foundational type of Christ, 'our passover sacrificed for us.'
